endorsements.quote: Stakeholders in implementation of AI tools in clinical practice should therefore familiarize themselves with the relevant methods and metrics for clinical evaluation and devise strategies to verify performance claims prior to tool introduction, and should continuously monitor performance during routine usage ( 64 ).

Re-evaluation of AI model performance using updated local data sets at specified intervals, but at least annually, may be an appropriate monitoring mechanism for models where gathering real-time data on model performance is limited (quantification, workflow enhancement, etc.) or in instances where patient safety will not be immediately impacted ( 80 ).

Institutions should develop a clearly defined escalation and resolution strategy when monitoring detects model failure or performance drift occurs that defines the notification and action plan, and the mode of operation while the model performance is being assessed and the cause of model failure determined.

Of course, vendors will have performed testing and quality assurance of the respective AI tools during regulatory approval, but purchasers should consider validation of the AI’s performance on a local dataset, and adjust parameters if needed prior to implementation in clinical practice.
This process should be repeated whenever relevant changes are made to the AI software or the equipment used in combination with the AI.

At a minimum, the characteristics of local data should be compared with those of the test data (a typical example might be where a model has been tested only on one manufacturer’s MRI scanner, but will be used on a scanner made by a different manufacturer).

Hence, parameters that are radiologist-facing, including positive and negative predictive values for the disease prevalence are more relevant than overall accuracy, Area Under the Curve (AUC), or sensitivity/specificity.
Thirdly, impressive, or “WOW cases,” should be identified to demonstrate the AI model’s value to users and stakeholders.

Finally, continuous user education throughout the lifecycle of AI utilization and monitoring radiologist AI usage and the combined accuracy of radiologist plus AI are instrumental in ensuring optimal patient care.

Therefore, as the use of AI becomes more prevalent and the AI tools being deployed become more diverse, institutions using AI should establish ongoing performance oversight as one function of a local AI governance process ( 78 ).
It cannot be simply assumed by user sites that intended benefits introduced by a manufacturer’s deployment of the latest version of a model automatically generalize to the local practice.

Training healthcare professionals in recognizing failure modes and offering a simple mechanism to disable autonomous AI when necessary is essential to avoid unchecked errors that could jeopardize patient care.

Transparency requires provision of clear information about an AI system’s capabilities and limitations, in particular the purpose for which the systems are intended, the conditions under which they can be expected to function as intended and the expected level of accuracy in achieving the specified purpose.
The concept of transparency should also extend to patients being made aware if AI systems are being used.

In situations where no such open data exist, developers should determine the baseline clinical performance, and compare the AI performance with existing or approved software, or radiologist multi-reader control data.

Two common errors in solution performance reporting include a failure to report a range of expected performance —lower quality solutions often report a single summary accuracy figure—and not reporting specific failure conditions and errors , with lower quality solutions selectively highlighting the best diagnoses made by their systems.

In the broader AI safety community, there is a strong embrace of Model Cards or System Cards , in which in-depth analyses of limitations, errors, and biases are explicitly reported, often entirely separate from the primary report of system performance ( 44 , 45 ).
Return on investment (RoI) and cost–benefit analyses should be planned and carried out to ensure the viability of the planned AI integration.
Identification of relevant changes in input parameters could trigger the re-evaluation process described above for periodic monitoring.
Strategies for real-world monitoring of AI in clinical practice should take into account the type of AI model being used and the risk to patient safety if the model performance declines.

Other targets for monitoring include changes in input metadata (e.g. equipment manufacturer, magnetic field strength or number of CT detectors), other relevant examination parameters and relevant demographic data about individual patients, since deviation of any or several of these from manufacturer specifications can result in degraded performance.
At a very minimum, a clear reporting procedure for unexpected errors to the vendor, with named responsible contact personnel, should be established and made easily accessible to clinical end users.

Of course, vendors will have performed testing and quality assurance of the respective AI tools during regulatory approval, but purchasers should consider validation of the AI’s performance on a local dataset, and adjust parameters if needed prior to implementation in clinical practice.

For any AI tool to be successfully integrated into clinical practice, stakeholders should first clearly identify areas that need improvement and define relevant key performance indicators ( 52 , 53 ).

unlisted_practices: Regulators should require an explicit post-market quality assurance plan from AI developers.
Regulators should draw clear categories between advisory, semi-automated, and automated AI systems, requiring a deeper evidence base for greater autonomy.
Regulators should encourage public model card transparency from AI developers.
Developers should involve clinicians early in the design of AI tools and target unmet clinical needs.
Developers of AI with poor explainability should provide a higher standard of empirical evidence, including external multi-centre data and prospective real-world evaluation.
Radiologists should receive continuous education on AI capabilities, limitations, and failure scenarios.
Integrate AI tools into existing clinical workflow and information systems to avoid additional user workload.
Enable radiologists to modify AI results in PACS and send corrected results to the vendor.
Autonomous AI should be designed so its actions are transparent, identifiable, and discoverable.
Use input distribution checks and comparison across multiple AI models to gain earlier insight into autonomous AI accuracy.
Assess AI error risk by considering error frequency, detectability, correctability, and impact.
Limit AI models to exam subsets with higher disease prevalence to reduce false positives.
Appoint a local AI champion and use change management to promote AI adoption.

screen.reason: This is a multi-society consensus statement/guideline providing practical recommendations for purchasing, implementing, and monitoring AI tools in radiology.
